solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Drink and hot dog after spending penny

indicators.note: money you have spent is no longer with you, so once the penny is spent the dog has lost it

parts.note: H = hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone nips to the loo, then comes back to a drink and a hot dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spending a penny' is British slang for going to the toilet, which is the picture the surface leans on; in the wordplay it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooch is slang for cheap or illicitly made liquor, so a drink by example.

clue.text: Falcon is extremely tedious for keen birdwatchers, perhaps

parts.note: the hobby is a small falcon

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its first and last letters are wanted

parts.note: first and last letters of TEDIOUS

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's grumble that falcons are dull.
explanation.walkthrough: The falcon fits the birdwatching surface perfectly, which hides that the bird's name is also a word for a pastime. 'Perhaps' flags birdwatchers as only one kind of enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen birdwatchers pursue a pastime, so they are one example of the answer.

clue.text: Concerning prisoner in prison camp

parts.note: of = concerning, as in 'tales of the sea'
an old lag is a long-serving convict

explanation.surface: A report about a prisoner held in a camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container instruction but only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oflag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for officers, such as Colditz.

clue.text: Investigation about Duke's representation of manhood

indicators.note: about means around, so the investigation goes around the duke

parts.note: a hearing is an official inquiry

explanation.surface: An inquiry into how a duke is portrayed as a man.
explanation.walkthrough: HEA-D-RING: the duke sits inside the hearing. The answer is obscure: a ring worn in the hair by Zulu men once they reached full adult status.
explanation.definitionFit: The Zulu headring was worn by married men as a badge of maturity, so it stood for manhood.

clue.text: Right after litigation, women damaged garden equipment

indicators.note: right comes after litigation in the finished word, trailing it as part of the jumble
something damaged is knocked out of shape

parts.note: used as printed, then rearranged with R

explanation.surface: A legal dispute, and then some women wreck the garden kit.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the women and the R are jumbled; the litigation stays intact at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain example: the machine that cuts the lawn is standard garden equipment.

clue.text: Dead on time? No

definitions.meaning: used of someone recently dead, before their name

explanation.surface: A curt verdict on whether something died punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a little question and answer: asked if it was on time, the reply is no.
explanation.definitionFit: Used before a name, the word means recently dead; in everyday use it means not on time.

clue.text: Publication supporting club is source of disagreement

indicators.note: in a down clue a support holds from beneath, so the publication goes below the club

parts.note: a wedge is a golf club

explanation.surface: A club newsletter that causes rows among members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a society with a newsletter; it is the golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A political term for a divisive topic used to split opponents' supporters, so a source of disagreement.

clue.text: Procedure of drug overdose

explanation.surface: A grim account of how a drug overdose happens.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'procedure' look like a hospital treatment; it is simply a way of doing things.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a set way of doing something.

clue.text: Very parsimonious treasurer initially with good intentions

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the treasurer's opening letter is used

explanation.surface: A stingy club treasurer who at least has his heart in the right place.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a character sketch of a tight-fisted treasurer, so 'very' looks like a mere intensifier rather than a word to be replaced.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for an act done with good intentions even if it misfires.

clue.text: Fanatical Scotsman regularly wild

parts.note: Rab, a Scots form of Robert, stands for any Scotsman

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every second letter of wild is taken

parts.note: second and fourth letters of wIlD

explanation.surface: A fervent, untamed Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords use common Scottish first names such as Ian, Mac and Rab to stand for a Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, the rage of a mad dog applied to views held with fanatical zeal.

clue.text: Made steady jockey stable lad

indicators.note: as a verb, to jockey is to jostle and manoeuvre for position, so the letters shift about

explanation.surface: A jockey and a stable lad calming a horse at the yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jockey' is a noun in the racing picture, but it works as the verb, jostle. 'Steady' and 'stable' both sit in the surface to misdirect.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballast is weight added low in a ship to keep it steady, so adding it made the ship steady.

clue.text: Fundamentalist thanks liberal

explanation.surface: A hardliner thanks a liberal, an unlikely exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets a fundamentalist against a liberal as opposites, yet the liberal supplies half the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The singular of Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist movement in Afghanistan.

clue.text: In tent, turn back what culture may have produced

indicators.note: the reversed turn is placed inside the tent

parts.note: a yurt is a round felt tent of the Central Asian steppe

indicators.note: going back means the word runs from its end to its start

parts.note: a go = a turn, as in 'your go'

explanation.surface: A camper inside a tent wondering what civilisation has produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Culture' reads as civilisation or the arts; here it is a bacterial culture, which is what thickens milk.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint by example: live bacterial cultures added to milk produce it.

clue.text: Warped behaviour breaks contract

indicators.note: to break into something is to split it open, so behaviour splits the contract

parts.note: a deed is a legal contract

explanation.surface: Twisted conduct leads someone to break an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks contract' reads as a single phrase for reneging; 'breaks' is the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: bent or twisted out of its proper shape.

clue.text: Break into building and suffer injury stealing clubs

indicators.note: what is stolen is taken in and held, so the injury takes the clubs inside

explanation.surface: A burglar breaks in, gets hurt, and makes off with some golf clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The C slips in just before RIB. The phrase is old thieves' cant, in which a crib was a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Old criminal slang for burgling a house, crib being cant for a dwelling.

clue.text: No promises broken in garbled statement

indicators.note: the promises are broken in the surface, and broken letters come apart and reassemble

explanation.surface: Someone backs out of promises in a muddled statement.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the definition describes the kind of wordplay that swaps sounds, such as 'a blushing crow' for 'a crushing blow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A slip that swaps the initial sounds of words, named after Rev. William Spooner, so a garbled statement.

clue.text: Subtle meanings in obvious jokes

parts.note: as in 'have you heard the one about...'

explanation.surface: Subtle meanings buried in crude jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets subtle against obvious; the less familiar step is a joke being called a 'one'.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, the extra harmonics above a note: implied meanings beyond the literal.

clue.text: Rear is fine part of the body

parts.note: an arm is a body part

explanation.surface: Someone admiring a shapely backside as their best feature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rear' looks like a noun, a bottom, and the body-part surface keeps it that way; it is the verb, to raise animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: to farm livestock is to rear it.

clue.text: Irrational individual had misinterpreted boring question

indicators.note: a word misinterpreted is read wrongly, so its letters come out in a different order
boring means drilling into, so the jumbled letters go inside the question

parts.note: a matter = a question, as in 'a matter of taste'
HAD rearranged, going in after the first letter

explanation.surface: Someone got a dull question wrong and seemed irrational.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like dull; it means drilling into. The character is from Alice in Wonderland, where he is simply 'the Hatter'.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: the Hatter at the tea party is the byword for irrational behaviour.

clue.text: Incapacitated, carried out clutching fur

indicators.note: to clutch is to hold tightly, so one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: did = carried out, as in 'did the job'

explanation.surface: An injured person being carried out, still clutching a fur coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carried out' pictures a stretcher; it is simply a past tense of 'do'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: put out of action.

clue.text: Stop baseball team returning

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the team's name runs backwards

explanation.surface: A plea to halt a baseball team's comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returning' reads as the team coming home, not as a direction to read the name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense: to stem a flow of blood or water is to stop it.

clue.text: Well-versed expert hosts charming Democrat

indicators.note: a host has guests inside his house, so the expert takes the other word inside

explanation.surface: A knowledgeable pundit entertaining a charming Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the Democrat is the guest, but it only tags on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Acquainted with a subject means familiar with it, so well-versed.

clue.text: Go pale, affected in crowded city

indicators.note: the first piece is placed in the second

parts.note: a wen is a cyst; William Cobbett called London 'the Great Wen'
hit = affected, as in 'hit by the news'

explanation.surface: Someone blanches, overwhelmed by a crowded city.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords use wen for any overgrown, crowded city, after Cobbett's nickname for London.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to become white or pale.

clue.text: Wife with better method of contraception

parts.note: 'my old Dutch' is Cockney slang for one's wife

explanation.surface: A wife with a more reliable form of birth control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' reads as an adjective; it is the verb, to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: British name for a contraceptive diaphragm.

clue.text: Entrance to building opened by new benefactor

indicators.note: a door opened by something has it standing in the gap, so the letter sits inside

explanation.surface: A building's entrance ceremonially opened by its generous patron.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a patron cutting the ribbon; 'opened by' is the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: one who gives money or goods.

clue.text: Possibly ram Greek character

parts.note: the surface offers a sheep; read it as a young sheep's da (dad), since a ram may be a father
the surface suggests a person from Greece; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A guess that a Greek figure might be a ram.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as LAMB DA: a lamb's da, its dad, could be a ram. 'Possibly' allows that not every ram is a father.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambda is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: What might be seen in jackboOTs?

definitions.text: What might be seen in jackboOTs?

parts.note: two letters are printed in capitals, so they are large

explanation.surface: A question about who wears jackboots.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed capitals are the wordplay: jackboOTs shows a big OT. Read whole, jackboots evoke fascist thugs, and an intolerant person might be found in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackboots symbolise authoritarian bullying, so an intolerant person is who might be seen wearing them.

clue.text: Beware large hole in the ground

definitions.meaning: a hollow in rock or earth

explanation.surface: A warning shouted at the edge of a pit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word was British public-school slang, shouted by a lookout when a master approached.
explanation.definitionFit: Schoolboy slang for 'look out', and in ordinary English a large natural hollow underground.

clue.text: Piece of music at last in 4/4 time

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the final letter of 'in' is used

explanation.surface: A musician's note about a piece written in common time.
explanation.walkthrough: 4/4 reads as a time signature in the musical surface; it is simply a fraction equal to one.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a composition for nine performers is one kind of piece of music.

clue.text: Nobleman punches to avenge shiner

indicators.note: a punch drives into its target, so the nobleman goes into the other word

parts.note: to right a wrong is to avenge it

explanation.surface: A nobleman throws punches to repay a black eye.
explanation.walkthrough: A shiner is slang for a black eye, which the fighting surface supports; here it means literally something that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: the lamp at the back of a vehicle is something that shines.

clue.text: Part of heel-bone sore when twisted a bit

indicators.note: the letters wanted are only part of the words that follow
twisted round, so the hidden letters are read in reverse

parts.note: the run from the second E of heel to the R of sore

explanation.surface: Complaint of a heel that is sore after being twisted a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit' reads as 'slightly'; it is a coin, as in a threepenny bit. The anatomy surface makes 'part of' look like a bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Bit as in threepenny bit means a coin, and this was a medieval English gold coin.

clue.text: Inhibit weightwatcher? Not I

indicators.note: 'Not I' says the I is absent, so it is taken out

explanation.surface: A dieter insisting 'Not me' when urged to show restraint.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags weightwatcher as a definition by example: any dieter will do.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to discourage someone from acting.
